title: Nielsen's 10 Usability Heuristics — Visual Exam Revision
description: All ten of Jakob Nielsen's usability heuristics, animated with one running example (a food ordering app), plus a mnemonic to remember the order.

scenes.title: Intro
lines: How do you judge whether an interface is good, without running a big user study?
Jakob Nielsen gave us ten rules of thumb, called usability heuristics.
We will walk through all ten using one simple example: a food ordering app.

scenes.title: The 10 at a glance + mnemonic
lines: Here are the ten, in order.
Visibility of system status. Match with the real world. User control and freedom. Consistency and standards. Error prevention.
Recognition rather than recall. Flexibility and efficiency. Aesthetic and minimalist design. Help with errors. And help and documentation.
To remember the order, take the first letters: V, M, U, C, E, R, F, A, H, H.
Very Many Users Complain, Errors Really Frustrate And Hurt Humans.

scenes.title: 1. Visibility of system status
lines: Heuristic one. Visibility of system status.
You tap Place Order. If nothing happens, you panic and tap again.
A good design always keeps users informed about what is going on, through feedback, within a reasonable time. Ideally, immediately.
No action with consequences should happen without telling the user.
Clear, continuous feedback makes interactions predictable, and that builds trust.

scenes.title: 2. Match between system and real world
lines: Heuristic two. Match between the system and the real world.
Speak the user's language. Not system-oriented terms like this error code.
Say: your card was declined. Use familiar words, phrases and concepts.
Follow real-world conventions, so information appears in a natural and logical order. A shopping cart, a trash can.
Never assume your words match your users' words. User research reveals their terminology and mental models.

scenes.title: 3. User control and freedom
lines: Heuristic three. User control and freedom.
Users often choose functions by mistake. Oops, the pizza got removed from the cart.
They need a clearly marked emergency exit, without an extended dialogue. Here, one tap on undo.
So: support undo and redo, and show a clear way out, like a Cancel button.
And make that exit clearly labeled and easy to discover.

scenes.title: 4. Consistency and standards
lines: Heuristic four. Consistency and standards.
Users should not have to wonder whether different words or actions mean the same thing. Save, store and keep? Pick one.
Internal consistency means consistency within your own product, or your family of products.
External consistency means following conventions of the industry or the web at large. Like the cart icon at the top right.
Breaking consistency increases cognitive load, because users must learn something new. Consistency improves learnability.

scenes.title: 5. Error prevention
lines: Heuristic five. Error prevention.
Good error messages are important, but the best designs prevent problems from happening in the first place.
Either remove the error-prone condition, like greying out past delivery dates, or ask for confirmation before a risky action.
Prioritize: prevent high-cost errors first, then the little frustrations.
Avoid slips with helpful constraints and good defaults. Reduce memory burden, support undo, and warn users.

scenes.title: 6. Recognition rather than recall
lines: Heuristic six. Recognition rather than recall.
Think of an exam. Fill in the blank is recall. Multiple choice is recognition. Which is easier?
Minimize memory load by making elements, actions and options visible.
Users should not have to remember information from one screen to another. Show recent orders, labels and menus.
Offer help in context, instead of a long tutorial to memorize.

scenes.title: 7. Flexibility and efficiency of use
lines: Heuristic seven. Flexibility and efficiency of use.
A beginner orders by browsing through menus, step by step.
An expert taps one shortcut: reorder last meal. Accelerators like keyboard shortcuts and gestures, hidden from novices, speed up experts.
So one design caters to both inexperienced and experienced users.
Also allow personalization, customization, and tailoring of frequent actions.

scenes.title: 8. Aesthetic and minimalist design
lines: Heuristic eight. Aesthetic and minimalist design.
Interfaces should not contain information that is irrelevant or rarely needed.
Every extra unit of information competes with the relevant units, and reduces their visibility.
So strip the noise. Keep content and visuals focused on the essentials and the primary goal.
Minimalist does not mean ugly. It means nothing distracts from what matters.

scenes.title: 9. Recognize, diagnose, recover from errors
lines: Heuristic nine. Help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors.
This message tells the user nothing.
Error messages should use plain language with no error codes, say precisely what the problem is, and constructively suggest a solution.
Give them a visual treatment, like red color and a highlighted field, so users notice them.
Exam tip: heuristic five is before an error happens. Heuristic nine is after.

scenes.title: 10. Help and documentation
lines: Heuristic ten. Help and documentation.
Ideally the system needs no explanation at all.
But when help is needed, it should be easy to search, and focused on the user's task.
Keep it concise, and list the concrete steps to carry out.

scenes.title: Recap
lines: Quick recap. Very Many Users Complain, Errors Really Frustrate And Hurt Humans.
Visibility, Match, User control, Consistency, Error prevention.
Recognition, Flexibility, Aesthetic, Help with errors, Help and documentation.
Picture the food app for each one, and you will remember all ten.
